lesson.title: Instance Methods: Behavior Tied to One Specific Object
lesson.summary: An instance method is any ordinary method that takes self as its first parameter, letting it read or change the data belonging to whichever one object called it, which is why two objects of the same class can hold completely different state.
lesson.body:
Every method you've written so far, __init__, area, bark, has actually belonged to a specific category called instance methods, and now it's worth naming that category explicitly. An instance method is a method whose first parameter is self, which means it's bound to one particular instance (one particular object) of the class every time it's called. This is the ordinary, everyday kind of method, and it's worth naming clearly now because later you'll meet class methods and static methods, which deliberately don't work this way.

The defining feature of an instance method is that it can look at and change the attributes of the one object it was called on, without affecting any other object built from the same class. That independence is what makes objects useful for modeling real, separate things, two dogs, two circles, two bank accounts, each with its own data even though they share identical behavior defined once in the class.

```python
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

a = BankAccount("Mia", 100)
b = BankAccount("Sam", 50)

a.deposit(25)
print(a.balance)
# Output: 125
print(b.balance)
# Output: 50
```

Both a and b are BankAccount objects, built from the exact same class and the exact same deposit method. But when a.deposit(25) runs, self is bound specifically to a, so self.balance += amount changes only a's balance, from 100 to 125. Object b never enters the picture at all, its balance stays untouched at 50. That's the whole point of an instance method: the same code, self.balance += amount, produces a different, correct result depending on which object it was called through. If methods couldn't do this, every object of a class would be forced to share identical data, which would make classes far less useful for representing distinct, individual things in your program.
